trial_name: SORT — Albumin in Spontaneous Bacterial Peritonitis (1999)
journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
citation: Sort P, Navasa M, Arroyo V, et al. Effect of intravenous albumin on renal impairment and mortality in patients with cirrhosis and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. N Engl J Med. 1999;341(6):403-9.
one_liner: In patients with cirrhosis and SBP, adding albumin to antibiotics reduced renal impairment (33% to 10%) and in-hospital mortality (29% to 10%) without affecting infection resolution.

pico.population: Hospitalised adults with cirrhosis and ascites diagnosed with SBP (ascitic PMN >250/mm³), age 18-80, excluding shock, GI bleeding, severe encephalopathy, creatinine >3 mg/dL, CVP <4 mm Hg if dehydration suspected.
pico.intervention: Intravenous cefotaxime (dose-adjusted to creatinine) plus albumin 20%: 1.5 g/kg within 6 h, then 1 g/kg on day 3 (day‑3 labs before albumin).
pico.outcome: Primary: renal impairment during hospitalisation (nonreversible >50% rise in BUN/creatinine with thresholds BUN >30 mg/dL or creatinine >1.5 mg/dL if no baseline renal failure). Secondary: in‑hospital mortality, 3‑month mortality, resolution of infection, hospital stay.

background.existing_knowledge: SBP is a frequent, high‑mortality complication of decompensated cirrhosis with ascites. Even with effective antibiotics, ~1/3 develop renal impairment — the strongest short‑term prognostic marker. Albumin was known to be effective as a plasma expander in other cirrhosis contexts (e.g., post‑paracentesis circulatory dysfunction).
background.knowledge_gap: The role of adjunctive albumin to prevent renal impairment and improve survival in SBP was uncertain.
background.hypothesis: In adults with cirrhosis and SBP, early intravenous albumin added to standard antibiotic therapy would reduce renal impairment and mortality compared to antibiotics alone.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, parallel‑group, open‑label controlled trial; 7 university hospitals in Spain; enrolment Nov 1995–Sep 1997; central review committee verified analyses.
methods.setting: 7 university hospitals in Spain, hospitalised patients with cirrhosis and ascites diagnosed with SBP.

inclusion: Ascitic‑fluid polymorphonuclear count >250/mm³ (bedside inoculation into blood‑culture bottles)
exclusion: Antibiotics within 1 week pre‑diagnosis (except prophylactic norfloxacin)
Findings suggestive of organic nephropathy (proteinuria/haematuria/abnormal renal ultrasound)
If dehydration suspected, central venous pressure <4 mm Hg

methods.intervention: Intravenous cefotaxime (dose‑adjusted to creatinine) plus albumin 20%: 1.5 g/kg within 6 h after enrolment, then 1 g/kg on day 3 (day‑3 labs drawn before albumin). SBP resolution defined as disappearance of infection signs and ascitic PMN ≤250/mm³.
methods.comparison: Intravenous cefotaxime alone (same dose adjustment). Antibiotic modification permitted in non‑responders. Diuretics and therapeutic paracentesis prohibited until infection resolution; partial paracentesis (3 L) occurred pre‑resolution in 7 patients (3 control, 4 albumin). After infection resolution, prophylactic norfloxacin 400 mg/day continued; tense ascites treated with total paracentesis plus albumin (6–8 g/L removed) irrespective of original allocation.
methods.blinding: Unblinded (open‑label). Randomisation performed using sealed envelopes; investigators unaware of assignment at the point of randomisation.
methods.sample_size_power: Power calculation: assuming renal impairment in ~30% with cefotaxime, 50 patients/group required to detect a 25% between‑group difference in renal impairment during hospitalisation with two‑sided α=0.05, β=0.20 (80% power). Final analysis intention‑to‑treat.
methods.primary_outcome: Renal impairment during hospitalisation: nonreversible deterioration with >50% rise in BUN/creatinine, meeting thresholds (BUN >30 mg/dL or creatinine >1.5 mg/dL if no baseline renal failure; >50% rise if baseline renal failure).
secondary_outcomes: Resolution of SBP infection (disappearance of infection signs and ascitic PMN ≤250/mm³)
methods.follow_up: In‑hospital follow‑up; post‑discharge weekly for 1 month then monthly to 90 days from enrolment.

headline_bullets: Albumin reduced renal impairment from 33% to 10% (ARR 23%, NNT ≈4) and in‑hospital mortality from 29% to 10% (ARR 19%, NNT ≈5).
Infection resolution was similar (94% vs 98%, P=0.36).
Renal impairment was tightly linked to death: 78% in‑hospital mortality with renal impairment vs 3% without (P<0.001).
Between‑group separation in BUN and creatinine was evident from day 3, without differences in MAP.

outcomes_table.note: Nonreversible >50% rise in BUN/creatinine meeting thresholds.
Commonest cause: combined liver + renal failure (13 control vs 5 albumin).
7 patients lost to follow‑up (4 control, 3 albumin); denominator‑based calculation assumes non‑informative missingness.
Initial cefotaxime success 84% vs 90%; remaining resolved after antibiotic modification.

subgroup_table.note: Low risk; absolute numbers not provided — percentages only.

safety: No adverse effects attributed to albumin infusion were reported.

domains.notes: Randomisation list generated by SAS, sealed envelopes at each hospital; investigators unaware of assignments at the point of randomisation; open‑label thereafter (risk of performance bias).
Unblinded design could influence co‑interventions (e.g., timing of paracentesis, escalation of supportive care), but key endpoints were objective (renal biochemistry and mortality).

ITT stated; 2 patients in albumin arm did not meet inclusion criteria and were withdrawn from protocolised albumin but included in final analysis (n=126). 7 patients lost to 90‑day follow‑up (4 vs 3); 90‑day mortality calculated as known deaths / total randomised, assuming non‑informative missingness.

After infection resolution, both groups could receive albumin with total paracentesis (6–8 g/L removed) — a pre‑specified post‑SBP pathway that would tend to reduce between‑group separation rather than inflate it.
No significant differences; renal failure at enrolment 44% (control) vs 40% (albumin); Child–Pugh 10±0.2 both groups.
Renal impairment required nonreversible deterioration with >50% rise in BUN/creatinine meeting thresholds; differs from contemporary AKI staging systems.

BUN significantly lower in albumin group days 3–9 (e.g., day 6: 36±3 vs 22±3 mg/dL, P=0.003); creatinine lower days 6–9; sodium higher (e.g., day 3: 130±1 vs 134±1 mmol/L, P=0.001); MAP not different.
Multivariable logistic regression used to identify independent predictors; adjusted ORs reported for renal impairment and in‑hospital mortality.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate‑to‑strong internal validity: randomisation and objective endpoints support causal inference; clear physiological separation; limitations from open‑label design, modest sample size, pre‑randomisation exclusions, and era‑specific renal outcome definition.

domains.notes: Hospitalised cirrhosis with SBP in Spanish university centres; high baseline severity (Child–Pugh ~10, renal failure ~40%); excluded shock, GI bleeding, severe encephalopathy, creatinine >3 mg/dL, and hypovolaemia (CVP <4 mm Hg).

Cefotaxime‑based therapy was standard at the time; modern antimicrobial choices may differ. Albumin dosing is feasible, but cost and availability may limit adoption in low‑resource settings. Findings most directly apply to haemodynamically stable SBP without major acute competing insults; less generalisable to ICU‑level septic shock SBP or multifactorial AKI.

external_validity.verdict: Good generalisability for classical inpatient SBP without shock or advanced renal disease; extrapolation to modern nosocomial SBP with multidrug resistance and severely unstable presentations requires clinical judgement.

strengths: Clinically decisive endpoints (renal impairment and mortality).
Mechanistic alignment (renin activity and renal outcomes).
Clear between‑group separation in renal physiology and outcomes.
limitations: Moderate sample size with wide confidence intervals for adjusted effects.
Restrictive exclusions selecting a haemodynamically stable phenotype.
Era‑specific renal impairment definition (not aligned with modern AKI staging).
Incomplete 90‑day mortality ascertainment for 7 patients with denominator‑based calculation.

critical_appraisal.summary: This trial demonstrates a large, clinically meaningful reduction in renal impairment and mortality with adjunctive albumin in SBP, likely by preventing circulatory dysfunction and renal vasoconstriction. The effect is consistent and supported by objective endpoints and mechanistic data, but the open‑label design and small sample introduce some uncertainty.
strengths: Objective endpoints and clear physiological separation.
Consistent effect across renal and mortality outcomes.

sections.authors_conclusion: Albumin plus antibiotics significantly reduces renal impairment and mortality in patients with cirrhosis and SBP. The benefit is mediated by prevention of circulatory dysfunction and renal failure, independent of infection resolution. Albumin should be considered a standard adjunct to antibiotics in SBP.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: This trial changed practice: albumin 1.5 g/kg day 1 and 1 g/kg day 3 should be given to patients with cirrhosis and SBP, especially those at high risk of renal impairment.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Hospitalised adults with cirrhosis and SBP, without shock, GI bleeding, severe encephalopathy, or creatinine >3 mg/dL.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Albumin does not replace antibiotics; it does not improve infection resolution but prevents renal failure and death.
implementation_caveats: Cost and resource availability may limit use in low‑resource settings.
Identify high‑risk patients using baseline bilirubin and creatinine to target therapy.
Do not delay antibiotics; albumin is adjunctive.

controversies.notes: Editorial highlighted that the most plausible strategy is to prioritise albumin for higher‑risk SBP presentations given the clear risk stratification by baseline biochemistry and the cost/dose burden.
Correspondence argued low‑risk subsets (low bilirubin, preserved renal function) have very low renal impairment rates, raising the possibility of overtreatment if albumin is applied indiscriminately.
The lack of blinding was an inherent vulnerability; however, the magnitude of effect on objective endpoints and mechanistic consistency reduce pure performance‑bias explanations.

Later syntheses and practice guidelines in hepatology broadly incorporated the concept that albumin plus antibiotics reduces SBP‑associated renal dysfunction and mortality, and commonly recommend the same weight‑based dosing schedule.

unresolved_questions: Optimal albumin dosing in low‑risk SBP.
Generalizability to nosocomial SBP with multidrug‑resistant organisms.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In patients with cirrhosis and SBP, albumin 1.5 g/kg then 1 g/kg reduces renal impairment and death by >60% and should be standard care.
